explanation.surface: An exclamation about a gang of rabble-rousers who are trouble to handle.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning sticks of wood are literal hot stuff, and agitators who stir up unrest are the figurative kind.

indicators.note: enclosed says the abbreviation for foot wraps round the bill's letters

parts.note: FT is the standard abbreviation for foot as a measure
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to pay the bill, which has been sent in an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot the bill' reads as one idiom meaning pay, but it splits into FT and AC (account), with 'enclosed' putting AC inside FT. 'Indeed' is the definition, as in the phrase 'in fact'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In fact' and 'indeed' are interchangeable emphatic adverbs, so the noun stands for the truth being asserted.

clue.text: Don't' give this grass the chance to grow under our feet

definitions.text: Don't' give this grass the chance to grow under our feet

parts.words: Don't' give this grass the chance to grow under our feet
parts.note: the saying 'don't let the grass grow under your feet' means don't dawdle; the grass in question is a marsh plant whose name also means hurry

explanation.surface: A gardener warns against letting the lawn get overgrown underfoot.
explanation.definitionFit: The marsh plant shares its name with haste, the cure for letting grass grow under one's feet.

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Hamlet, Gertrude marries Claudius, the brother of her late husband

explanation.surface: A note on a royal wedding in a famous play.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudius was the brother of Gertrude's dead husband, making him her relative by marriage before he became her spouse.

parts.note: workers on strike typically demand a pay increase, a rise

explanation.surface: A call to rise up, made as a demand by workers on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get up' is the definition; 'a strikers' demand' is A plus RISE, the British word for a pay raise.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand up or get out of bed is to rise from lying or sitting.

parts.note: hops are gathered in Kent fields, but a 'hop' is also an informal dance, so hop-gatherers are people who come together to dance

explanation.surface: Asking where the people who pick hops for beer would gather.
explanation.definitionFit: A hop is an old word for a social dance, held in a public venue built for dancing.

explanation.surface: A fish leaves its mark at the foot of a cliff.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep rocky outcrop in northern England, the parrot-wrasse once called scarus, and a healed wound's trace all share this name.

indicators.note: in places the word for time inside the word for the middle

parts.note: the middle of something is its centre
taken as written

explanation.surface: A runner's split time partway through a middle-distance race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle distance' reads as an athletics term, but 'the middle' gives CENTRE and 'distance' is the definition; 'in' puts TIME inside CENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundredth of a metre is a small unit of length, i.e. of distance.

clue.text: Hardly the place to cultivate red oranges !

definitions.text: Hardly the place to cultivate red oranges

indicators.note: to cultivate is to work the soil and turn it over, so the letters of the fodder are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Oranges would never grow in such an English flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultivate' rearranges RED ORANGES, and the whole clue is also the definition: a bed of red roses is no place for an orange grove.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot given over to a flowering shrub is clearly not the spot to grow citrus fruit.

clue.text: A discount's turned over to the caretakers

indicators.note: turning over the letters of a discount's mixes them into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Building caretakers are passed a reduction in price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' rearranges A DISCOUNTS; the possessive 's supplies its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Keepers or guardians of a building look after it, as caretakers do.

explanation.surface: Someone asks whose turn it is to pay for the drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A responsibility or duty is a burden; split in two, the letters say a round of drinks is paid for by us.

explanation.surface: Someone among the queen's courtiers is a pin-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A small curd tart is called by this name, as is an unmarried lady who attends a queen at court.

clue.text: Mean to give the mice an outside chance?

definitions.text: to give the mice an outside chance?

explanation.surface: A plan to let some mice have a slim chance of winning.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingy people were said to save the rind trimmed from their dairy food; that rind, the outside, is what mice would get.

parts.note: a punch-up seen as clenched hands inside shirt cuffs, the ends of the sleeves

explanation.surface: A slapstick comedy routine performed without jackets.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare-knuckle fighting is done with clenched hands poking out of shirt cuffs.

clue.text: The detail must be varied so interest is aroused

indicators.note: varied tells us the letters of detail must are changed into another order

explanation.surface: A writer's advice: vary the detail to keep the reader interested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be varied' looks like instruction, but 'be varied' rearranges DETAIL MUST, the word 'must' included.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stimulated has been excited or roused into activity.

parts.note: a foreign, Latin phrase that itself means among other things

explanation.surface: Something described as unusual, among several qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag, foreign to English, translates as 'among other matters'.

clue.text: Woodworker belongs to a mutual admiration society

definitions.text: belongs to a mutual admiration society

explanation.surface: A carpenter is a member of a club that praises its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A lumberjack rolls timber; in politics, trading favours or praise with allies is called log-rolling.

parts.note: a fill-in-the-gap quotation from Keats's poem beginning 'In a ...-nighted December'

explanation.surface: A line from a Keats poem about a gloomy winter night.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a poetic form meaning dismal or bleak, filling the gap in Keats's opening line.

parts.note: the Athenian whose name is in the title of a Shakespeare play, 'of Athens'

explanation.surface: A nobleman of ancient Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's misanthrope gives his name to the play's title, so he is the titled citizen of Athens.

clue.text: In such a wind it's possible to feel cargo shifting !

indicators.note: cargo shifting in a ship's hold moves about, so the letters of feel cargo are rearranged

explanation.surface: In a storm at sea you can feel the ship's load moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifting' rearranges FEEL CARGO; the definition is 'such a wind'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind of force 8 on the Beaufort scale is strong enough to class as a gale.

parts.note: someone who 'played ball' with the occupying Germans under the wartime Vichy regime in France

explanation.surface: A former sportsman from the French spa town.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Vichy rule, French people who cooperated with the German occupiers were branded traitors for working with the enemy.

clue.text: It's large enough in even the smallest samples

indicators.note: in signals the word sits inside the letters of samples

explanation.surface: A claim that even the tiniest test portions are big enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside SAMPLES, whose middle letters spell the answer; 'even the smallest' implies dropping just the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Plentiful or sufficient means there is enough of something.

parts.note: the middle day of the week is named after Woden, the Norse chief god under another name

explanation.surface: A deity honoured in the middle of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: Wednesday is Woden's day, and Woden is the Germanic form of the Norse chief god.

clue.text: The 3rd March issue of " Little Women "

definitions.text: The 3rd March issue of " Little Women "

parts.words: The 3rd March issue of " Little Women "
parts.note: not a magazine date: the third of the four March sisters, the children (issue) of the family in Alcott's novel

explanation.surface: A dated edition of a classic American novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy are the March girls, and the third-born is the gentle sister who dies young.

clue.text: It sounds just the place to have one's fortune told

definitions.text: It sounds just the place to have one's fortune told

parts.words: It sounds just the place to have one's fortune told
parts.note: a village fair has a fortune-teller's tent, and its name is said like the word for destiny

explanation.surface: A recommendation of somewhere to visit a fortune-teller.
explanation.definitionFit: A summer fair often has a palm-reader, and its name sounds like 'fate', which is one's fortune.

parts.note: a flap is a state of panic
a doodle is an idle drawing

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses an anxious sketch as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panic drawing?' reads as a question about a picture, but it is FLAP (panic) followed by DOODLE (drawing).
explanation.definitionFit: This old word for foolish talk means much the same as balderdash.

parts.note: 'come clean' is confess, but literally soapy froth is what we wash with

explanation.surface: A confession made in the company of others.
explanation.definitionFit: Soapy lather is what people wash with to get clean.

parts.note: the clue refers to the Vichy clue at 20; de Gaulle's forces fought on against the occupiers and despised those who sided with them

explanation.surface: Soldiers scornful of someone who sided with the enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: De Gaulle's wartime movement fought on from exile and scorned the Frenchmen who worked with the occupiers.
